course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 5
unit.description: Follow Manifest Destiny and the Mexican–American War, the sectional conflict over slavery, the election of 1860 and secession, the Civil War, and Reconstruction and its failure from 1844 to 1877.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: Election of 1860 and Secession
lesson.summary: How the election of 1860 split the parties, why most slave states seceded after Lincoln's victory, and how the firing on Fort Sumter began the Civil War.
learningGoals: Explain how the Democratic split and Lincoln's victory without Southern electoral votes produced the secession crisis.
Explain the reasons that Southern leaders gave for secession and Lincoln's response.
Explain how Fort Sumter and Lincoln's call for troops determined which states joined the Confederacy.
lesson.bigIdea: Lincoln was elected on a free-soil platform without any Southern electoral votes, and the Southern states that seceded in response formed a Confederacy that the Union refused to accept.
lesson.context: The CED asks you to describe the effects of Lincoln's election. For each event, ask what Southern leaders feared would follow and how Lincoln answered them.

sections.title: The election of 1860

blocks.text: The Democratic Party split in 1860. Northern Democrats nominated Stephen Douglas, who supported popular sovereignty, and Southern Democrats nominated Vice President John C. Breckinridge of Kentucky, who demanded federal protection of slavery in the territories. John Bell of Tennessee ran on the ticket of the Constitutional Union Party, which asked voters to support the Union and the Constitution. The Republicans nominated Abraham Lincoln, who opposed the spread of slavery but promised not to interfere with it in the states where it existed.

Abraham Lincoln's victory on the Republicans' free-soil platform in the presidential election of 1860 was accomplished without any Southern electoral votes. He won only about 40 percent of the popular vote, and his name was not even on the ballot in most Southern states, but he carried nearly all of the free states, which gave him a majority of the electoral votes.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: The election was lawful under the rules of the Constitution. Lincoln won the Electoral College without a majority of the popular vote, and the Southern states left because of what they expected his party to do, not because of any fraud.

sections.takeaway: A divided Democratic Party and a united North elected Lincoln without a single Southern electoral vote.

sections.title: Secession

blocks.text: After a series of contested debates about secession, most slave states voted to secede from the Union. Southern leaders argued that the Union was a compact among sovereign states that could be withdrawn from, and that the election of a president pledged to stop the spread of slavery threatened their rights and their way of life. Several states' declarations named the protection of slavery as a central reason. South Carolina left the Union in December 1860, and by February 1861 Mississippi, Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana, and Texas had followed. Delegates from these seven states formed the Confederate States of America and chose Jefferson Davis as president.

Efforts to avoid the break failed. The Crittenden Compromise would have extended the line at 36°30′ to the Pacific and protected slavery south of it, but Lincoln refused to accept any plan that allowed slavery to spread into the territories. In his First Inaugural Address in March 1861, Lincoln said that he had no purpose to interfere with slavery in the states where it existed, that the Union was perpetual, and that the issue of civil war was in the hands of those who would break it.

sections.takeaway: Seven states seceded to protect slavery, and Lincoln rejected both secession and any compromise that allowed slavery to spread.

sections.title: Fort Sumter and the Upper South
sections.conceptTitle: Fort Sumter and the Upper South

blocks.text: Confederate forces took most federal forts in the South, but the Union held Fort Sumter in Charleston harbor. When Lincoln sent supplies to the fort, Confederate batteries fired on it on April 12, 1861, and the garrison surrendered. Lincoln called for 75,000 volunteers to put down the rebellion.

The call for troops pushed the Upper South to a decision. Virginia, Arkansas, Tennessee, and North Carolina seceded, which brought the Confederacy to eleven states. Four slave states, Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky, and Missouri, stayed in the Union and are called the border states. Lincoln worked to keep them loyal because their location and resources were important to the Union.

sections.takeaway: Fort Sumter began the war, and Lincoln's call for troops brought four more states into the Confederacy.

connections.title: From secession to war
connections.body: With eleven states in the Confederacy, the two sides had to mobilize for a long war. Topic 5.8 follows the military conflict.
connections.transferQuestion: How did Lincoln's statements in 1858 about slavery and the Union compare with his statements in 1861?
connections.feedback: A strong answer notes that in both periods he opposed the spread of slavery and promised not to interfere with it in the states, while in 1861 he also argued that the Union was perpetual and that secession was not lawful.
